title: Architecture Decision: Selecting an Event Delivery Platform
subtitle: As we split the order domain into microservices, we compare three options for an asynchronous event delivery platform between services. We evaluate them on throughput, operational burden, and cost, then present our recommendation and the rationale behind it.
footer: Source: Platform Architecture Guild · Decision date 2026-06-07 · Proposed by platform-arch@example.com · Status: Pending approval

sections.html:
Background and Constraints

The current monolith integrates services through synchronous REST calls, and cascading failures occur at peak load (8,000 orders per second). The new platform must meet three requirements: process a peak of 12,000 msg/s at p99 < 200ms, guarantee at-least-once delivery, and be operable by a team of 2 SREs. The three options under evaluation are Apache Kafka (self-hosted), Amazon SQS + SNS (managed), and NATS JetStream (lightweight).

options.name: A. Apache Kafka (Self-hosted)
pros: Handles 12,000 msg/s comfortably, with linear horizontal scaling
Log retention and replay make failure recovery and reprocessing easy
cons: High learning curve for ZooKeeper / KRaft and broker operations
Significant always-on cost even with a minimal 3-node setup
Risk of overloading operations with only 2 SREs

options.name: B. SQS + SNS
pros: Fully managed, with zero broker operations
SNS fan-out makes topic subscriptions easy
Pay-as-you-go keeps costs low during light traffic
cons: Standard queues offer no ordering guarantee (FIFO caps at 3,000 msg/s)
Message retention is limited to a maximum of 14 days
Vendor lock-in and limited low-level control

options.name: C. NATS JetStream (Lightweight)
pros: Single binary with fast startup and lightweight operations
cons: No in-house operational expertise and limited track record
Cluster operations and backups must be built in-house

sections.title: Recommendation: Option B (SQS + SNS)
sections.body: The requirement ceiling (12,000 msg/s) is comfortably met by standard queues, and this option best satisfies the zero-operational-burden constraint. Only payment events that require ordering guarantees are isolated to a FIFO queue (within 3,000 msg/s). Kafka's high throughput is overkill, while NATS carries the risk of insufficient operational expertise. Considering cost, operations, and requirement fit overall, we adopt Option B.

sections.html: Figure: Messages that fail delivery are parked in the dead-letter queue (DLQ) after the maximum retries and monitored separately via alerts. The success path completes with the consumer's ACK.

tabs.label: B. SQS + SNS (Recommended)
tabs.body:
B. Amazon SQS + SNS — Managed Architecture

Events published to an SNS topic are fanned out to multiple SQS queues. Each consumer group subscribes to a dedicated queue and achieves at-least-once delivery via visibility timeouts and a retry policy. FIFO queues are used only for the payment domain, where ordering is mandatory.

When to Use

  • Ideal for organizations that cannot dedicate an SRE to operations
  • Not suited to cases requiring broad global ordering guarantees
  • Lets AWS automatically absorb traffic spikes

Key Metrics

ItemValue
Standard queue limitUnlimited
FIFO queue limit3,000 msg/s
Max retention period14 days
p99 latency35 ms

Terraform Excerpt

resource "aws_sns_topic" "order_events" {
  name = "order-events"
}

resource "aws_sqs_queue" "inventory" {
  name                       = "inventory-consumer"
  visibility_timeout_seconds = 30
  redrive_policy = jsonencode({
    deadLetterTargetArn = aws_sqs_queue.inventory_dlq.arn
    maxReceiveCount     = 5
  })
}

tabs.label: A. Apache Kafka
tabs.body:
A. Apache Kafka — Self-hosted Architecture

Build a cluster of 3 brokers (KRaft mode) with a replication factor of 3. Consumer parallelism is controlled by the number of partitions, and reprocessing is possible thanks to log retention. Schema Registry ensures schema compatibility. Throughput far exceeds the requirements, but operational cost is the central concern.

When to Use

  • Recommended only when a dedicated operations team can be secured
  • Powerful if event sourcing / reprocessing is a core requirement
  • Well suited to sharing streams across multiple teams

Key Metrics

ItemValue
Max throughput~1.2M msg/s
p99 latency9 ms
Minimum node count3
Operational burdenHigh

Note: KRaft has eliminated the ZooKeeper dependency, but the operational burden of rebalancing, disk management, and monitoring remains substantial.

tabs.label: C. NATS JetStream
tabs.body:
C. NATS JetStream — Lightweight Architecture

It starts from a single binary, and JetStream provides stream persistence and redelivery. A 3-node cluster ensures high availability, and sub-millisecond latency is a strength. Operations are lightweight, but there is no in-house track record, so onboarding and building out monitoring infrastructure incur an initial cost.

When to Use

  • Strong choice when low latency is the top priority and you want lightweight operations
  • Adopting it with zero in-house expertise is high risk
  • A good fit for edge / IoT messaging

Key Metrics

ItemValue
Max throughput~800K msg/s
p99 latency4 ms
Minimum node count3
Operational burdenMedium

Note: A managed offering (Synadia Cloud) also exists, but compliance for this requirement mandates operation within our own VPC, so it was evaluated on the assumption of a self-managed cluster.
